# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Review: *Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem* (Varga & Holm, Comment)

Sections 1–5 are strong. The comment brings new evidence from the microdata and largely confirms the concerns raised from the working paper alone. Its final conclusion, though, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact", is not supported by its own numbers, and it leaves out the strongest evidence against it.

## Arithmetic

Most figures check out:

- **Table 2:** 95.1/0.8 = +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%, and 95.4/86.1 = +10.8%. The hours ratios match the stated hours (34.6/40.3 = 0.859; 34.8/40.4 = 0.861).
- **Real revenue:** 1.014/1.041 = 0.974, a fall of about 2.6%.
- **Sign test:** 19 of 23 managers' indices exceeding the record-based figure is unlikely by chance (two-sided p ≈ 0.003).

Two figures don't reconcile.

**The hours decomposition doesn't add up.** Baseline was 40.3 hours, about 8.06 per day. Four days at +0.7 hours each, plus 1.6 hours on the day off, gives about 36.6 hours. The reported figure is 34.6. The reported total implies only about +0.2 hours per day on the remaining days. Perhaps the +0.7 is per week, or measured against a different reference. Either way the components should be corrected or explained.

**The novelty extrapolation lands at month 9, not 10.** Energy fell 0.32 SD between months 3 and 6. At that rate, the remaining 0.29 SD disappears by about month 8.7. This is minor; the bigger problems with §6 are below.

## Real contributions

1. **Attrition (§1).** This is the most important new finding. The working paper said withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". If the microdata show seven of nine withdrew *after* the schedule began, mostly citing workload, the original description is wrong in a way that flatters the result. The Halden authors should respond.
2. **Manager versus records (§2).** A systematic gap of 3.8 points is good evidence of sponsor bias. It is also framed fairly: the authors explicitly say they do not suggest bad faith.
3. **Actual hours (§3).** Measuring actual hours from time-tracking logs turns a stated limitation into an estimate.
4. **Sectoral claims (§5).** This section correctly identifies that the per-hour metric guarantees a gain whenever output stays above 80.

## Problems

### 1. Attrition is described but never corrected

The abstract says "correcting the first three [problems]" gives 10.8%, and the first three include attrition. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is not adjusted for anywhere.

The comment also never estimates how much attrition matters. A crude worst-case bound suggests it matters less than the rhetoric implies. Suppose all nine withdrawals had zero per-hour gain, meaning an output index of 80, and weight by organisation:

- (61 × 98.7 + 9 × 80) / 70 ≈ 96.3
- 96.3 / 0.8 = +20.4% per scheduled hour

Even under that assumption, attrition removes only about 3 points of the 23.4%. The bound is rough because the withdrawn organisations' sizes are unknown, but it should be reported. Without it, the abstract's claim that four problems "account for most of the reported gain" overstates attrition's role.

The revenue problem in §4 doesn't affect the per-hour estimate at all. So it also can't be one of the problems accounting for the gain.

### 2. Table 2 mixes samples

The rows use 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations, so differences between rows combine two things: the correction itself and changes in which organisations are included. The table's "successive corrections" framing implies a clean decomposition, and it isn't one.

All four specifications should be computed within the 17-organisation subset:

- manager-reported output with scheduled hours;
- record-based output with scheduled hours;
- manager-reported output with actual hours;
- record-based output with actual hours.

That would show how much each correction contributes. The data note acknowledges the subsets are non-random, but the table's presentation works against that caveat.

Two related gaps:

- **Weighting.** The pilot used employee-weighted means. The comment doesn't say whether its means are weighted the same way, which matters for comparing against 98.7.
- **Uncertainty.** There are no confidence intervals anywhere. The 10.8% figure rests on 17 organisations and needs one.

### 3. The corrected estimate matches the best randomised evidence, and the comment omits it

This is the central problem. After correction, the 17-organisation subset shows output down 4.6%, actual hours down 13.9%, and a per-hour gain of +10.8%. The Varden trial's case-processing stratum shows output per FTE down 2.1%, actual hours down 13%, and a per-hour gain of +12.5% (CI +6.9 to +18.4).

Varden meets every standard the comment itself recommends:

- randomisation;
- record-based output;
- actual hours;
- no reliance on self-selected organisations.

The comment calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature". But it never mentions the case-processing stratum from the same trial, which shows a per-hour gain of almost exactly the size the comment's corrections leave behind.

Two independent sources converging on a gain of roughly 11–12% is evidence *against* the "entirely an artifact" conclusion. Citing one stratum of Varden and not the other is selective.

Varden's gain has its own caveats. With only 7 versus 7 offices, its confidence intervals are probably too narrow. And part of the gain may come from removing meetings rather than from people working harder. Neither caveat makes the gain an artifact.

### 4. The novelty argument is asserted, not tested

**Energy is not output.** A decay in self-reported energy doesn't show that output per hour decayed.

**The direct test is available and wasn't run.** The pilot collected a monthly output index, and the comment's authors hold the microdata. Time-tracking logs and records may also be monthly. If output per actual hour declined from month 1 to month 6, that would support novelty. If it was flat, it would count against it.

**A straight line through two points is not a forecast.** Energy could plausibly level off rather than return to baseline.

**Varden counts against pure novelty.** Its gain held at nine months in offices assigned to the change, which is less fertile ground for enthusiasm than volunteers who opted in. Varden staff did know they were in a trial, so a novelty effect isn't ruled out there.

**The burden-of-proof argument is applied unevenly.** §6 says those claiming a durable effect must prove it. Yet §6 itself asserts novelty on weaker evidence than the correlation §7 dismisses.

### 5. The meetings section mischaracterises Varden and conflicts with §6

**It wasn't a selected subgroup.** The seven offices are the entire treated case-processing stratum. The analysis was unregistered and post hoc, and the Varden authors said so themselves. They also reported that the correlation rests on seven offices and registered a confirmatory test.

**The scepticism about r = 0.71 across seven offices is fair.** The 95% CI runs from roughly −0.09 to 0.95, so it cannot establish a mechanism.

**Other evidence supports the meetings hypothesis.** In Halden, 47 of 58 managers independently mentioned cutting meetings. In Varden, treated case-processing offices spent 3.3 fewer hours per week in meetings than control offices.

**Meetings and novelty predict different things.** A gain from removing meetings is a structural change, not an effort surge, so there is no reason it should fade. The comment can't dismiss the meetings explanation as unproven while treating its own speculative explanation as the default. The defensible position is that both are open hypotheses, and the 24-month Varden follow-up can help separate them.

### 6. The conclusion overreaches the data note

The data note says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole". The conclusion then generalises to "the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes", meaning all schemes, from one self-selected pilot. And the comment's own best estimate is a positive gain of about 11%.

What the evidence supports is two-sided:

- **Presence-bound work:** reduced hours reduce output. Halden's retail and hospitality data and Varden's counter stratum agree on this.
- **Backlog-based work:** a per-hour gain of roughly 10–12% survives correction for output measurement and actual hours, in both the corrected Halden subset and the randomised Varden trial. Whether it lasts, and whether it comes from removing low-value time or from effort, is unresolved.

## Smaller points

- **Time-tracking may still undercount hours.** §3 notes that some day-off work probably isn't logged. That would push the per-hour gain lower still. It deserves a sentence, since it supports the comment's direction.
- **CPI is a rough deflator for firm revenue.** Sector or producer price indices would be better. The point about real revenue stands regardless.
- **"Less than half the reported 23.4%"** is true, but only just: 10.8 against a threshold of 11.7.
- **Retail and hospitality records come from three organisations.** The −11.2% figure needs that caveat inline, not only in the data note.
- **Recommendations.** These are sound. Adding "report confidence intervals and pre-specify corrections" would make them consistent with the comment's own critique.

## Overall

Sections 1–3 should stand, and the attrition finding in particular needs a reply from the Halden authors. The comment needs four changes:

1. Correct for attrition, or at least bound its effect, and fix the abstract's claim about it.
2. Recompute Table 2 within a single subset and add confidence intervals.
3. Test novelty directly using the monthly microdata.
4. Engage with Varden's case-processing result and replace "entirely an artifact" with a conclusion that matches the corrected estimates.

I can draft a revised abstract and conclusion, or a short reply from the Halden authors' perspective.
